newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission launches debate on flexible working.
newsitem.headline: Commission launches debate on flexible working.

text.p: The European Commission is due on Wednesday to launch a wide-ranging debate on ways of introducing more flexible working practices without compromising worker security.

The initiative coincides with separate discussions between European Union officials, trade unions and employers on a code of conduct that will oblige employers to inform their workers in plenty of time before introducing company restructuring measures.

On Wednesday, the Commission is expected to adopt a green paper (discussion document) entitled "Partnership for a new organisation of work", which examines why working practices are changing and how policy needs to change to allow for more flexibility without making jobs even more insecure.

According to the draft green paper, the EU has better prospects for economic growth now than it has seen in years but unless EU firms start replacing old rigid hierarchical structures by more flexible working practices they will lose this competitive edge.
Companies need to update their workers' skills to keep pace with advances in technology and changing markets, the paper says.
They need to introduce more flexible working time arrangements and change their wage systems accordingly, it continues.

But the document acknowledges that European enterprises have been slow to alter the way they operate and that some workers fear such changes may result in increasingly precarious employment conditions, such as short-term contracts and the growing use of freelance workers as a way of reducing employer's social security contributions.

European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn is due to present the paper to European social affairs ministers when they meet in Luxembourg on Thursday, and hold a series of discussions on new policy guidelines with employers, trade unions and public authorities between now and November.

Flynn is expected to stress on Wednesday that moves towards greater flexibility will succeed only if employees participate alongside employers and the public authorities in drafting new policies on working practices and if there is trust on all sides.
Keith Richardson, secretary-general of the European Round Table of Industrialists, said flexibility and deregulation were necessary to create jobs.
"Unemployment is happening because Europe is not modernising quickly enough," Richardson told Reuters.

"We don't want a complete jungle but there are too many rules...We need new forms of labour which are fair to everybody involved and the current situation is not fair, particularly to all those people who can't get jobs of any kind."

Moves to establish an EU code of conduct on worker consultation in the case of factory closures may go some way to improving trust, although it remains to be seen whether the social partners will agree to binding rules.

The existing EU directive on collective redundancies was "very vague" on the issue of worker consultation and the Commission would welcome clearer guidelines, Flynn's spokeswoman Barbara Nolan told a news conference on Tuesday.

The Commission last month accused French car maker Renault of breaching two EU directives on factory closures by deciding to close its Belgian plant at Vilvoorde, with the loss of over 3,000 jobs, without first negotiating with its workers or notifying the public authorities in advance.
Nolan said the Commission might recommend the introduction of stricter sanctions against companies which breached the rules, a proposal which has until now not won the support of EU governments.
